paragraphs.heading: What basalt is
paragraphs.text: Basalt is a fine-grained volcanic rock. It forms when runny lava rich in magnesium and iron cools quickly. This happens at the surface of a rocky planet or moon, or very near it. Basalt accounts for more than 90% of the volcanic rock on Earth. Basaltic magmas inside Earth are thought to come from the upper mantle, so the chemistry of basalt offers clues to processes deep in the planet's interior.

paragraphs.heading: Why the lava runs
paragraphs.text: Molten basalt has a relatively low silica content, between 45% and 52%. That gives the lava a low viscosity. Its viscosity is around 10⁴ to 10⁵ cP, similar to ketchup, though still far higher than water at about 1 cP. The lava flows move rapidly and can spread over great areas before they cool and harden. Flood basalts are thick stacks of many such flows. They can cover hundreds of thousands of square kilometres and are the most voluminous of all volcanic formations.

paragraphs.heading: Where the magma comes from
paragraphs.text: On Earth, most basalt is made by decompression melting of the mantle. High pressure in the upper mantle, from the weight of the rock above, raises the melting point of mantle rock, so nearly all of the upper mantle is solid. But that solid rock is ductile: it slowly deforms under high stress. When tectonic forces make hot mantle rock creep upward, the pressure on it falls. Its melting point can then drop far enough that the rock partly melts, and the melt is basaltic magma.

paragraphs.heading: Where it happens
paragraphs.text: Decompression melting can happen in several tectonic settings: continental rift zones, mid-ocean ridges, above geological hotspots, and back-arc basins. Subduction zones make basalt too: there, mantle rock rises into a wedge of mantle above a descending slab. As the slab goes down it gives off water vapor and other volatiles, which lower the melting point further and increase the amount of melting. Each setting produces basalt with its own distinctive characteristics.

paragraphs.heading: What it looks like
paragraphs.text: Basalt is usually dark grey to black, owing to a high content of augite or other dark pyroxene minerals. Some basalts are quite light in colour because they hold a lot of plagioclase. Basalt often contains larger crystals, called phenocrysts, set in a finer-grained matrix; they formed before the magma was brought to the surface. It also often contains vesicles. As magma decompresses on its way up, gases dissolved in it bubble out, and the erupted lava then hardens before those gases can escape. When vesicles make up a substantial part of the rock's volume, the rock is called scoria.

paragraphs.heading: A twin, and other worlds
paragraphs.text: Basalt has a slow-cooling twin. Coarse-grained gabbro cools slowly, yet it shares the chemical composition and mineralogy of fine-grained, fast-cooling basalt. Basalt is also an important rock on other bodies in the Solar System. Most of the plains of Venus are basaltic, and those plains cover about 80% of the surface. The lunar maria are plains made of flood-basalt lava flows. On the surface of Mars, basalt is a common rock.
